  >   1:name: test-driven-development
  >   2:description: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code
  >   3:---
  >   4:
  >   5:# Test-Driven Development (TDD)
  >   6:
  >   7:## Overview
  >   8:
  >   9:Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.
  >  10:
  >  11:**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.
  >  12:
  >  13:**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**
  >  14:
  >  15:## When to Use
  >  16:
  >  17:**Always:**
  >  18:- New features
  >  19:- Bug fixes
  >  20:- Refactoring
  >  21:- Behavior changes
  >  22:
  >  23:**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
  >  24:- Throwaway prototypes
  >  25:- Generated code
  >  26:- Configuration files
  >  27:
  >  28:Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.
  >  29:
  >  30:## The Iron Law
  >  31:
  >  32:```
  >  33:NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
  >  34:```
  >  35:
  >  36:Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.
  >  37:
  >  38:**No exceptions:**
  >  39:- Don't keep it as "reference"
  >  40:- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
  >  41:- Don't look at it
  >  42:- Delete means delete
  >  43:
  >  44:Implement fresh from tests. Period.
  >  45:
  >  46:## Red-Green-Refactor
  >  47:
  >  48:```dot
  >  49:digraph tdd_cycle {
  >  50:    rankdir=LR;
  >  51:    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
  >  52:    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
  >  53:    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
  >  54:    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
  >  55:    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
  >  56:    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];
  >  57:
  >  58:    red -> verify_red;
  >  59:    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
  >  60:    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
  >  61:    green -> verify_green;
  >  62:    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
  >  63:    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
  >  64:    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
  >  65:    verify_green -> next;
  >  66:    next -> red;
  >  67:}
  >  68:```
  >  69:
  >  70:### RED - Write Failing Test
  >  71:
  >  72:Write one minimal test showing what should happen.
  >  73:
  >  74:<Good>
  >  75:```typescript
  >  76:test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  >  77:  let attempts = 0;
  >  78:  const operation = () => {
  >  79:    attempts++;
  >  80:    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
  >  81:    return 'success';
  >  82:  };
  >  83:
  >  84:  const result = await retryOperation(operation);
  >  85:
  >  86:  expect(result).toBe('success');
  >  87:  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
  >  88:});
  >  89:```
  >  90:Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
  >  91:</Good>
  >  92:
  >  93:<Bad>
  >  94:```typescript
  >  95:test('retry works', async () => {
  >  96:  const mock = jest.fn()
  >  97:    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
  >  98:    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
  >  99:    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  > 100:  await retryOperation(mock);
  > 101:  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
  > 102:});
  > 103:```
  > 104:Vague name, tests mock not code
  > 105:</Bad>
  > 106:
  > 107:**Requirements:**
  > 108:- One behavior
  > 109:- Clear name
  > 110:- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)
  > 111:
  > 112:### Verify RED - Watch It Fail
  > 113:
  > 114:**MANDATORY. Never skip.**
  > 115:
  > 116:```bash
  > 117:npm test path/to/test.test.ts
  > 118:```
  > 119:
  > 120:Confirm:
  > 121:- Test fails (not errors)
  > 122:- Failure message is expected
  > 123:- Fails because feature missing (not typos)
  > 124:
  > 125:**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.
  > 126:
  > 127:**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.
  > 128:
  > 129:### GREEN - Minimal Code
  > 130:
  > 131:Write simplest code to pass the test.
  > 132:
  > 133:<Good>
  > 134:```typescript
  > 135:async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  > 136:  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  > 137:    try {
  > 138:      return await fn();
  > 139:    } catch (e) {
  > 140:      if (i === 2) throw e;
  > 141:    }
  > 142:  }
  > 143:  throw new Error('unreachable');
  > 144:}
  > 145:```
  > 146:Just enough to pass
  > 147:</Good>
  > 148:
  > 149:<Bad>
  > 150:```typescript
  > 151:async function retryOperation<T>(
  > 152:  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  > 153:  options?: {
  > 154:    maxRetries?: number;
  > 155:    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
  > 156:    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  > 157:  }
  > 158:): Promise<T> {
  > 159:  // YAGNI

  >  22:

  >   1:
  >   2:Add to your Codex config (`~/.codex/config.toml`):
  >   3:
  >   4:```toml
  >   5:[features]
  >   6:multi_agent = true
  >   7:```
  >   8:
  >   9:This enables the multi-agent tools that skills like
  >  10:`dispatching-parallel-agents` and `subagent-driven-development` use.
  >  11:Which tools you get depends on the multi-agent version your model
  >  12:preset selects (current presets run V2; older ones run V1). Trust your
  >  13:actual tool list over any table — including this one — when they
  >  14:disagree.
  >  15:
  >  16:- **Spawning:** give children a clean context with
  >  17:  `spawn_agent {fork_turns: "none"}`; the default `"all"` copies your
  >  18:  entire transcript into the child. On Codex 0.145+, role files under
  >  19:  `~/.codex/agents/` attach to isolated forks via `agent_type`.
  >  20:  Full-history forks accept `model` and `reasoning_effort` overrides
  >  21:  (only `agent_type` is refused there) — isolated forks are the SDD
  >  22:  default for context hygiene, not because overrides require them.
  >  23:- **Fix rounds:** resume the implementer with `followup_task` — it
  >  24:  delivers your message, triggers a turn, and transparently reloads a
  >  25:  child the harness evicted. Never dispatch a fresh implementer on the
  >  26:  theory that a spawned agent cannot be messaged again; on V2 it
  >  27:  always can.
  >  28:- **Lifecycle:** V2 has no `close_agent`. Finished children are
  >  29:  evicted automatically when slots are needed; leaving them unclosed
  >  30:  costs nothing. Only V1 sessions have `close_agent` — there, close
  >  31:  reviewers when their review returns, and close each implementer
  >  32:  after its task's review passes.
  >  33:- **Model names:** never copy a model name from a skill, table, or old
  >  34:  session into `spawn_agent` without checking it against your current
  >  35:  spawn allowlist — V2 accepts only V2-capable presets and hard-errors
  >  36:  on the rest.
  >  37:
  >  38:## Waiting on children
  >  39:
  >  40:`wait_agent` is an event subscription, not a poll: a long wait wakes
  >  41:the moment a child produces mailbox activity, with the same latency as
  >  42:a short one. Short-timeout polling buys nothing and costs a tool call —
  >  43:and a context rebill — per poll. In measured sessions, roughly
  >  44:two-thirds of all wait calls were short polls that timed out.
  >  45:
  >  46:- While you still have local work, do not wait at all. A completed
  >  47:  child's final answer is pushed into your mailbox and arrives with
  >  48:  your next turn.
  >  49:- When you are genuinely idle with children outstanding, wait in
  >  50:  bounded stretches: `wait_agent` with `timeout_ms` 300000-600000
  >  51:  (5-10 minutes). After each stretch — wake or timeout — post one
  >  52:  status line, run `list_agents`, and chase any child that finished
  >  53:  without reporting. Never stack polls shorter than five minutes; the
  >  54:  event subscription wakes a bounded stretch just as fast as a short
  >  55:  one.
  >  56:- Completion mail cannot wake an idle controller (it is delivered
  >  57:  without triggering a turn); covering that idle window is
  >  58:  `wait_agent`'s only job. A stretch that times out with no activity
  >  59:  is your cue to reconcile, not to shorten the next stretch.
  >  60:
  >  61:## Model routing on spawns
  >  62:
  >  63:Every `spawn_agent` you issue — including when you are yourself a
  >  64:spawned child running a fan-out — sets `model` AND `reasoning_effort`
  >  65:explicitly, per the Model Selection rules of the skill you are
  >  66:executing. Setting `model` alone is a trap: the child's effort
  >  67:silently resets to that model's default, not to yours.
  >  68:
  >  69:Ask your human partner to add a machine-level backstop to
  >  70:`~/.codex/config.toml` so any spawn that slips through still routes to
  >  71:a deliberate tier instead of silently inheriting the session's most
  >  72:expensive model:
  >  73:
  >  74:```toml
  >  75:[agents]
  >  76:default_subagent_model = "<a mid-tier model from your spawn allowlist>"
  >  77:default_subagent_reasoning_effort = "medium"
  >  78:```
  >  79:
  >  80:## Environment Detection
  >  81:
  >  82:Skills that create worktrees or finish branches should detect their
  >  83:environment with read-only git commands before proceeding:
  >  84:
  >  85:```bash
  >  86:GIT_DIR=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
  >  87:GIT_COMMON=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
  >  88:BRANCH=$(git branch --show-current)
  >  89:```
  >  90:
  >  91:- `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON` → already in a linked worktree (skip creation)
  >  92:- `BRANCH` empty → detached HEAD (cannot branch/push/PR from sandbox)
  >  93:
  >  94:See `using-git-worktrees` Step 0 and `finishing-a-development-branch`
  >  95:Step 1 for how each skill uses these signals.
  >  96:
  >  97:## Codex App Finishing
  >  98:
  >  99:When the sandbox blocks branch/push operations (detached HEAD in an
  > 100:externally managed worktree), the agent commits all work and informs
  > 101:the user to use the App's native controls:
  > 102:
  > 103:- **"Create branch"** — names the branch, then commit/push/PR via App UI
  > 104:- **"Hand off to local"** — transfers work to the user's local checkout
  > 105:
  > 106:The agent can still run tests, stage files, and output suggested branch
  > 107:names, commit messages, and PR descriptions for the user to copy."]}

{"test-driven-development\writing-good-tests.md": ["  >   0:# Writing Good Tests
  >   1:
  >   2:**Load this reference when:** writing or changing tests, adding mocks, or
  >   3:adding cleanup/helper methods for tests.
  >   4:
  >   5:## Overview
  >   6:
  >   7:A test exists to catch a specific break. Two principles govern everything
  >   8:here:
  >   9:
  >  10:```
  >  11:1. Every test names the break it catches
  >  12:2. Every test exercises the real thing
  >  13:```
  >  14:
  >  15:Strict TDD produces both naturally: a test written first and watched
  >  16:failing against real code has already proven it can fail, and only earns
  >  17:a mock when the real dependency proves slow or external.
  >  18:
  >  19:## Principle 1: Name the Break
  >  20:
  >  21:Before writing the test body, answer: **what production change should
  >  22:make this test fail — and is that change a bug or a decision?** A test
  >  23:earns its place by catching a wrong branch, missing side effect, wrong
  >  24:argument, boundary case, or broken contract.
  >  25:
  >  26:**Derive expectations independently.** Use literals and hand-checked
  >  27:fixtures; table-driven tests with literal `want` values are the preferred
  >  28:shape. An expectation computed by the code under test — or its helpers —
  >  29:passes no matter what that code does:
  >  30:
  >  31:```typescript
  >  32:// ❌ Mirror assertion: the same builder computes both sides — always true
  >  33:const expected = buildSearchQuery({ tag: 'urgent' });
  >  34:expect(buildSearchQuery({ tag: 'urgent' })).toBe(expected);
  >  35:
  >  36:// ✅ Hand-derived literal
  >  37:expect(buildSearchQuery({ tag: 'urgent' })).toBe('tag:"urgent"');
  >  38:```
  >  39:
  >  40:**No change detectors.** If only intentional decisions can fail a test —
  >  41:a constant's value, exact message wording, private structure — it fires
  >  42:on redesign and sleeps through bugs. Test the behavior that depends on
  >  43:the decision: not `expect(MAX_RETRIES).toBe(5)` but "a failing call is
  >  44:retried 5 times and the 6th attempt never happens."
  >  45:
  >  46:**Behavior, not text.** Asserting that a script, skill, or config
  >  47:contains an exact line proves only that the source is the source. Run
  >  48:scripts against controlled inputs and assert outputs, side effects, or
  >  49:exit codes. Documents that instruct agents are tested by the consuming
  >  50:agent's behavior (superpowers:writing-skills); prose for humans earns no
  >  51:test at all.
  >  52:
  >  53:**Your code, not the framework.** Test the contract your code makes at
  >  54:its boundaries — the route you register, the query you emit, the payload
  >  55:you produce. Upstream mechanics are their maintainers' tests to write
  >  56:(the classic: asserting your router invokes a registered handler — that
  >  57:is the framework's test, not yours). When upstream behavior genuinely
  >  58:surprised you, write one narrow characterization test naming the
  >  59:assumption. The same boundary applies inside your code: constructors,
  >  60:getters, constants, and trivial forwarding earn tests only when they
  >  61:validate, normalize, default, derive, enforce, or cause side effects —
  >  62:otherwise assert the first consumer-visible result that depends on them.
  >  63:
  >  64:### Gate Function
  >  65:
  >  66:```
  >  67:BEFORE writing the test body:
  >  68:  Name the production change that would make this test fail.
  >  69:
  >  70:  Cannot name one            → redesign around an observable behavior
  >  71:  "The source text changed"  → run the artifact and assert its effects
  >  72:  Only intentional decisions → change detector; test the behavior
  >  73:                               that depends on the decision
  >  74:
  >  75:  Confirm the expected value is derived without the code under test.
  >  76:  IF it reuses the code's logic or helpers:
  >  77:    Replace it with a literal or hand-checked fixture
  >  78:```
  >  79:
  >  80:## Principle 2: Exercise the Real Thing
  >  81:
  >  82:**The mock earns no assertions.** A mock assertion passes when the mock
  >  83:is present and fails when it is absent — it says nothing about the
  >  84:component. Assert the real component's behavior; if the mock is what you
  >  85:are checking, unmock it or delete the assertion.
  >  86:
  >  87:```typescript
  >  88:// ✅ Real behavior
  >  89:expect(screen.getByRole('navigation')).toBeInTheDocument();
  >  90:
  >  91:// ❌ Mock existence
  >  92:expect(screen.getByTestId('sidebar-mock')).toBeInTheDocument();
  >  93:```
  >  94:
  >  95:**your human partner's correction:** "Are we testing the behavior of a
  >  96:mock?"
  >  97:
  >  98:**Mock at the right level.** Learn every side effect of the real method
  >  99:before replacing it; mock the slow or external operation and keep what
  > 100:the test depends on real. When unsure, run the test against the real
  > 101:implementation first and observe what actually needs to happen.
  > 102:
  > 103:```typescript
  > 104:// ❌ The mock swallows the config write that duplicate detection reads
  > 105:vi.mock('ToolCatalog', () => ({
  > 106:  discoverAndCacheTools: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined)
  > 107:}));
  > 108:
  > 109:// ✅ Mock only the slow server startup; the config write stays real
  > 110:vi.mock('MCPServerManager');
  > 111:```
  > 112:
  > 113:**Make doubles specific.** When arguments, call counts, or ordering are
  > 114:part of the contract, assert them — a fake that accepts anything verifies
  > 115:nothing. Give each branch (success, error, malformed) its own fixture or
  > 116:spy, so the wrong branch cannot satisfy the expectation.
  > 117:
  > 118:**Mirror real data completely.** Mock the complete structure as it exists
  > 119:in reality — all documented fields — not just the ones your test reads.
  > 120:Partial mocks fail silently when downstream code reads an omitted field:
  > 121:the test passes while integration breaks.
  > 122:
  > 123:**Production classes carry production methods only.** Cleanup that only
  > 124:tests need lives in test utilities, never as a `destroy()` on the
  > 125:production class. Ask: is this method called only from tests? Does this
  > 126:class own this resource's lifecycle? Wrong answers → test utility.
  > 127:
  > 128:**Prefer real components over complex mocks.** When mock setup outgrows
  > 129:the test logic, mocks miss methods the real components have, or tests
  > 130:break when the mock changes, switch to an integration test with real
  > 131:components. **your human partner's question:** "Do we need to be using a
  > 132:mock here?"
  > 133:
  > 134:### Gate Function
  > 135:
  > 136:```
  > 137:BEFORE adding a mock or test helper:
  > 138:  List the real method's side effects; keep the ones the test

  >   2:description: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes
  >   3:---
  >   4:
  >   5:# Systematic Debugging
  >   6:
  >   7:## Overview
  >   8:
  >   9:**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.
  >  10:
  >  11:**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**
  >  12:
  >  13:## The Iron Law
  >  14:
  >  15:```
  >  16:NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
  >  17:```
  >  18:
  >  19:If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.
  >  20:
  >  21:## When to Use
  >  22:
  >  23:Use for ANY technical issue:
  >  24:- Test failures
  >  25:- Bugs in production
  >  26:- Unexpected behavior
  >  27:- Performance problems
  >  28:- Build failures
  >  29:- Integration issues
  >  30:
  >  31:**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
  >  32:- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
  >  33:- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
  >  34:- You've already tried multiple fixes
  >  35:- Previous fix didn't work
  >  36:- You don't fully understand the issue
  >  37:
  >  38:**Don't skip when:**
  >  39:- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
  >  40:- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
  >  41:- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)
  >  42:
  >  43:## The Four Phases
  >  44:
  >  45:You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.
  >  46:
  >  47:### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation
  >  48:
  >  49:**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**
  >  50:
  >  51:1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
  >  52:   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
  >  53:   - They often contain the exact solution
  >  54:   - Read stack traces completely
  >  55:   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes
  >  56:
  >  57:2. **Reproduce Consistently**
  >  58:   - Can you trigger it reliably?
  >  59:   - What are the exact steps?
  >  60:   - Does it happen every time?
  >  61:   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess
  >  62:
  >  63:3. **Check Recent Changes**
  >  64:   - What changed that could cause this?
  >  65:   - Git diff, recent commits
  >  66:   - New dependencies, config changes
  >  67:   - Environmental differences
  >  68:
  >  69:4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**
  >  70:
  >  71:   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**
  >  72:
  >  73:   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
  >  74:   ```
  >  75:   For EACH component boundary:
  >  76:     - Log what data enters component
  >  77:     - Log what data exits component
  >  78:     - Verify environment/config propagation
  >  79:     - Check state at each layer
  >  80:
  >  81:   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
  >  82:   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
  >  83:   THEN investigate that specific component
  >  84:   ```
  >  85:
  >  86:   **Example (multi-layer system):**
  >  87:   ```bash
  >  88:   # Layer 1: Workflow
  >  89:   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
  >  90:   echo "IDENTITY: $([ -n "${IDENTITY:-}" ] && echo SET || echo UNSET)"
  >  91:
  >  92:   # Layer 2: Build script
  >  93:   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
  >  94:   printenv IDENTITY >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "IDENTITY in environment" || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"
  >  95:
  >  96:   # Layer 3: Signing script
  >  97:   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
  >  98:   security list-keychains
  >  99:   security find-identity -v
  > 100:
  > 101:   # Layer 4: Actual signing
  > 102:   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
  > 103:   ```
  > 104:
  > 105:   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)
  > 106:
  > 107:5. **Trace Data Flow**
  > 108:
  > 109:   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**
  > 110:
  > 111:   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.
  > 112:
  > 113:   **Quick version:**
  > 114:   - Where does bad value originate?
  > 115:   - What called this with bad value?
  > 116:   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
  > 117:   - Fix at source, not at symptom
  > 118:
  > 119:### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis
  > 120:
  > 121:**Find the pattern before fixing:**
  > 122:
  > 123:1. **Find Working Examples**
  > 124:   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
  > 125:   - What works that's similar to what's broken?
  > 126:
  > 127:2. **Compare Against References**
  > 128:   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
  > 129:   - Don't skim - read every line
  > 130:   - Understand the pattern fully before applying
  > 131:
  > 132:3. **Identify Differences**
  > 133:   - What's different between working and broken?
  > 134:   - List every difference, however small
  > 135:   - Don't assume "that can't matter"
  > 136:
  > 137:4. **Understand Dependencies**
  > 138:   - What other components does this need?
  > 139:   - What settings, config, environment?
  > 140:   - What assumptions does it make?
  > 141:
  > 142:### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing
  > 143:
  > 144:**Scientific method:**
  > 145:
  > 146:1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
  > 147:   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
  > 148:   - Write it down
  > 149:   - Be specific, not vague
  > 150:
  > 151:2. **Test Minimally**
  > 152:   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
  > 153:   - One variable at a time
  > 154:   - Don't fix multiple things at once
  > 155:
  > 156:3. **Verify Before Continuing**
  > 157:   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
  > 158:   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
  > 159:   - DON'T add more fixes on top
  > 160:
  > 161:4. **When You Don't Know**
  > 162:   - Say "I don't understand X"
  > 163:   - Don't pretend to know
  > 164:   - Ask for help
  > 165:   - Research more
  > 166:
  > 167:### Phase 4: Implementation
  > 168:
  > 169:**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**
  > 170:
  > 171:1. **Create Failing Test Case**
  > 172:   - Simplest possible reproduction
  > 173:   - Automated test if possible
  > 174:   - One-off test script if no framework
  > 175:   - MUST have before fixing
  > 176:   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests
  > 177:
  > 178:2. **Implement Single Fix**
  > 179:   - Address the root cause identified
  > 180:   - ONE change at a time
  > 181:   - No "while I'm here" improvements
  > 182:   - No bundled refactoring
  > 183:
  > 184:3. **Verify Fix**
  > 185:   - Test passes now?
  > 186:   - No other tests broken?
  > 187:   - Issue actually resolved?
  > 188:   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success
  > 189:
  > 190:4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
  > 191:   - STOP
  > 192:   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
  > 193:   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
  > 194:   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
  > 195:   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion
  > 196:
  > 197:5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**
  > 198:
  > 199:   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
  > 200:   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
  > 201:   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
  > 202:   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere
  > 203:
  > 204:   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
  > 205:   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
  > 206:   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
  > 207:   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?
  > 208:
  > 209:   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**
  > 210:
  > 211:   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.
  > 212:
  > 213:## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process
  > 214:
  > 215:If you catch yourself thinking:
  > 216:- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
  > 217:- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
  > 218:- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
  > 219:- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
  > 220:- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
  > 221:- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
  > 222:- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
  > 223:- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
  > 224:- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
  > 225:- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
  > 226:- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**
  > 227:
  > 228:**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**
  > 229:
  > 230:**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)
  > 231:
  > 232:## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong
  > 233:
  > 234:**Watch for these redirections:**
  > 235:- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
  > 236:- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
  > 237:- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
  > 238:- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
  > 239:- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working
  > 240:
  > 241:**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.
  > 242:
  > 243:## Common Rationalizations
  > 244:
  > 245:| Excuse | Reality |
  > 246:|--------|---------|
  > 247:| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
  > 248:| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
  > 249:| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
  > 250:| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
  > 251:| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
  > 252:| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
  > 253:| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
  > 254:| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |
  > 255:
  > 256:## Quick Reference
  > 257:
  > 258:| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
  > 259:|-------|---------------|------------------|
  > 260:| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
  > 261:| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
  > 262:| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
  > 263:| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |
  > 264:
  > 265:## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"
  > 266:
  > 267:If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:
  > 268:
  > 269:1. You've completed the process
  > 270:2. Document what you investigated
  > 271:3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
  > 272:4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation
  > 273:
  > 274:**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.
  > 275:
  > 276:## Supporting Techniques
  > 277:
  > 278:These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:
  > 279:
  > 280:- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
  > 281:- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
  > 282:- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling"]}

  >  27:- Performance problems
  >  28:- Build failures
  >  29:- Integration issues
  >  30:
  >  31:**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
  >  32:- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
  >  33:- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
  >  34:- You've already tried multiple fixes
  >  35:- Previous fix didn't work
  >  36:- You don't fully understand the issue
  >  37:
  >  38:**Don't skip when:**
  >  39:- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
  >  40:- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
  >  41:- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)
  >  42:
  >  43:## The Four Phases
  >  44:
  >  45:You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.
  >  46:
  >  47:### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation
  >  48:
  >  49:**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**
  >  50:
  >  51:1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
  >  52:   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
  >  53:   - They often contain the exact solution
  >  54:   - Read stack traces completely
  >  55:   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes
  >  56:
  >  57:2. **Reproduce Consistently**
  >  58:   - Can you trigger it reliably?
  >  59:   - What are the exact steps?
  >  60:   - Does it happen every time?
  >  61:   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess
  >  62:
  >  63:3. **Check Recent Changes**
  >  64:   - What changed that could cause this?
  >  65:   - Git diff, recent commits
  >  66:   - New dependencies, config changes
  >  67:   - Environmental differences
  >  68:
  >  69:4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**
  >  70:
  >  71:   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**
  >  72:
  >  73:   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
  >  74:   ```
  >  75:   For EACH component boundary:
  >  76:     - Log what data enters component
  >  77:     - Log what data exits component
  >  78:     - Verify environment/config propagation
  >  79:     - Check state at each layer
  >  80:
  >  81:   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
  >  82:   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
  >  83:   THEN investigate that specific component
  >  84:   ```
  >  85:
  >  86:   **Example (multi-layer system):**
  >  87:   ```bash
  >  88:   # Layer 1: Workflow
  >  89:   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
  >  90:   echo "IDENTITY: $([ -n "${IDENTITY:-}" ] && echo SET || echo UNSET)"
  >  91:
  >  92:   # Layer 2: Build script
  >  93:   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
  >  94:   printenv IDENTITY >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "IDENTITY in environment" || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"
  >  95:
  >  96:   # Layer 3: Signing script
  >  97:   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
  >  98:   security list-keychains
  >  99:   security find-identity -v
  > 100:
  > 101:   # Layer 4: Actual signing
  > 102:   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
  > 103:   ```
  > 104:
  > 105:   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)
  > 106:
  > 107:5. **Trace Data Flow**
  > 108:
  > 109:   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**
  > 110:
  > 111:   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.
  > 112:
  > 113:   **Quick version:**
  > 114:   - Where does bad value originate?
  > 115:   - What called this with bad value?
  > 116:   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
  > 117:   - Fix at source, not at symptom
  > 118:
  > 119:### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis
  > 120:
  > 121:**Find the pattern before fixing:**
  > 122:
  > 123:1. **Find Working Examples**
  > 124:   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
  > 125:   - What works that's similar to what's broken?
  > 126:
  > 127:2. **Compare Against References**
  > 128:   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
  > 129:   - Don't skim - read every line
  > 130:   - Understand the pattern fully before applying
  > 131:
  > 132:3. **Identify Differences**
  > 133:   - What's different between working and broken?
  > 134:   - List every difference, however small
  > 135:   - Don't assume "that can't matter"
  > 136:
  > 137:4. **Understand Dependencies**
  > 138:   - What other components does this need?
  > 139:   - What settings, config, environment?
  > 140:   - What assumptions does it make?
  > 141:
  > 142:### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing
  > 143:
  > 144:**Scientific method:**
  > 145:
  > 146:1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
  > 147:   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
  > 148:   - Write it down
  > 149:   - Be specific, not vague
  > 150:
  > 151:2. **Test Minimally**
  > 152:   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
  > 153:   - One variable at a time
  > 154:   - Don't fix multiple things at once
  > 155:
  > 156:3. **Verify Before Continuing**
  > 157:   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
  > 158:   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
  > 159:   - DON'T add more fixes on top
  > 160:
  > 161:4. **When You Don't Know**
  > 162:   - Say "I don't understand X"
  > 163:   - Don't pretend to know
  > 164:   - Ask for help
  > 165:   - Research more
  > 166:
  > 167:### Phase 4: Implementation
  > 168:
  > 169:**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**
  > 170:
  > 171:1. **Create Failing Test Case**
  > 172:   - Simplest possible reproduction
  > 173:   - Automated test if possible
  > 174:   - One-off test script if no framework
  > 175:   - MUST have before fixing
  > 176:   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests
  > 177:
  > 178:2. **Implement Single Fix**
  > 179:   - Address the root cause identified
  > 180:   - ONE change at a time
  > 181:   - No "while I'm here" improvements
  > 182:   - No bundled refactoring
  > 183:
  > 184:3. **Verify Fix**
  > 185:   - Test passes now?
  > 186:   - No other tests broken?
  > 187:   - Issue actually resolved?
  > 188:   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success
  > 189:
  > 190:4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
  > 191:   - STOP
  > 192:   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
  > 193:   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
  > 194:   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
  > 195:   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion
  > 196:
  > 197:5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**
  > 198:
  > 199:   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
  > 200:   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
  > 201:   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
  > 202:   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere
  > 203:
  > 204:   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
  > 205:   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
  > 206:   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
  > 207:   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?
  > 208:
  > 209:   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**
  > 210:
  > 211:   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.
  > 212:
  > 213:## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process
  > 214:
  > 215:If you catch yourself thinking:
  > 216:- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
  > 217:- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
  > 218:- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
  > 219:- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
  > 220:- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
  > 221:- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
  > 222:- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
  > 223:- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
  > 224:- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
  > 225:- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
  > 226:- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**
  > 227:
  > 228:**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**
  > 229:
  > 230:**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)
  > 231:
  > 232:## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong
  > 233:
  > 234:**Watch for these redirections:**
  > 235:- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
  > 236:- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
  > 237:- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
  > 238:- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
  > 239:- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working
  > 240:
  > 241:**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.
  > 242:
  > 243:## Common Rationalizations
  > 244:
  > 245:| Excuse | Reality |
  > 246:|--------|---------|
  > 247:| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
  > 248:| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
  > 249:| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
  > 250:| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
  > 251:| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
  > 252:| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
  > 253:| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
  > 254:| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |
  > 255:
  > 256:## Quick Reference
  > 257:
  > 258:| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
  > 259:|-------|---------------|------------------|
  > 260:| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
  > 261:| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
  > 262:| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
  > 263:| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |
  > 264:
  > 265:## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"
  > 266:
  > 267:If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:
  > 268:
  > 269:1. You've completed the process
  > 270:2. Document what you investigated
  > 271:3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
  > 272:4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation
  > 273:
  > 274:**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.
  > 275:
  > 276:## Supporting Techniques
  > 277:
  > 278:These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:
  > 279:
  > 280:- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
